newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Strong growth expected to slice UK PSBR.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Strong growth expected to slice UK PSBR.

text.p: Britain seems poised to borrow less under a likely Labour government with strong growth easing its public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) throughout 1997 and 1998, a Reuters survey showed on Monday.

From a survey of 32 economists and research institutions conducted between April 7 and 9, 26 gave numbers for PSBR. The average of these forecasts predicted a total deficit of around 18.7 billion sterling for fiscal year 1997/98, easing to around 14.9 billion in the following year.
The government's forecast for the 1996-7 fiscal year is 26.4 billion pounds. In the 11 months to February the deficit was 14.09 billion sterling.

Opposition Labour is widely tipped to topple the ruling Conservative party at the election on May 1, but Britons are unlikely to see a return to the tax-and-spend policies of previous Labour administrations, analysts said.

"Labour has been pretty up-front about fiscal policy. It has pledged to keep to the existing government's spending targets and I think it will want to be true to its word," said Mark Ramsden, UK economist at Stone and McCarthy Research.

Strong growth will also assist a new government's ability to control the PSBR, analysts said. An average of 29 economists in the Reuters poll showed gross domestic product growth peaking at 3.4 percent in the third quarter of 1997.
"That will help unemployment to continue falling which cuts a little bit of welfare spending and brings in quite a lot of revenue," said Andy Cates, UK economist at UBS.
David Bloom, UK economist at HSBC James Capel agreed. He predicted a 15 billion deficit in fiscal year 1997/98, slipping to just seven billion in 1998/99.
"Our growth forecast is higher than most at 4.25 pct this year so we expect receipts to be pretty punchy," he said.

"We have to believe that Labour will hold to their spending commitments. If you do get stronger growth...there's no reason why the PSBR shouldn't come down quite substantially over the next two years."
But other economists were concerned that robust growth would fail to take such a big bite out of the deficit.
Edmund Nonis, UK economist at Nikko Europe, predicted a 20 billion deficit in both 1997/98 and 1998/99.
"Our feeling is that any growth in economy will occur in areas that will not be highly revenue-generating for the government such as part-time work and contract work," he said.

And while Labour have said they will stick to the spending targets laid down by the current Conservative administration, there are still lingering fears that in the long run, Labour will have problems keeping the lid on expenditure.
"The big uncertainty is in the long term, whether Labour can hold down the rate of public spending," Stone and McCarthy's Ramsden said.
"The doubts must be greater under Labour, simply because their philosophy still favours the public sector."
